name: Data Structures
description: Learn how to store and organise data (lists, stacks, trees, graphs) and the classic algorithms that work on it.

blocks.html:
Algorithms & Big-O

What is an Algorithm?

An algorithm is a list of clear steps that solves a problem, like a recipe. A data structure is a way of storing data so that the algorithm can use it easily. Good programmers choose both together: the right structure makes the algorithm short and fast.

Two programs can give the same answer but one may take one second and the other one hour. To compare them we do not use a stopwatch, because every computer has a different speed. Instead we count how many steps the algorithm needs when the input gets bigger.

Big-O Notation

Big-O describes how the number of steps grows when the input size n grows. We ignore small details and keep only the biggest part. For example, 3n + 5 steps is just O(n), and n*n + n steps is O(n^2).

Big-ONameExample
O(1)ConstantRead items[0]
O(log n)LogarithmicBinary search in a sorted list
O(n)LinearAdd up every number in a list
O(n^2)QuadraticCompare every pair of items

From fastest to slowest growth: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n^2). A smaller growth rate is better when the data is large.

Counting Steps

Let us count steps with real code. The function first_item always does one thing. The function total visits each item once. The function count_pairs has a loop inside a loop, so it visits every pair.

blocks.code:
def first_item(items):
    return items[0]            # always 1 step

def total(items):
    steps = 0
    s = 0
    for x in items:            # runs n times
        s += x
        steps += 1
    return steps

def count_pairs(items):
    steps = 0
    for a in items:            # n times
        for b in items:        # n times for each a
            steps += 1
    return steps

for n in (10, 100, 1000):
    data = list(range(n))
    print(f"n={n}: O(1)=1 step, O(n)={total(data)} steps, O(n^2)={count_pairs(data)} steps")
blocks.output:
n=10: O(1)=1 step, O(n)=10 steps, O(n^2)=100 steps
n=100: O(1)=1 step, O(n)=100 steps, O(n^2)=10000 steps
n=1000: O(1)=1 step, O(n)=1000 steps, O(n^2)=1000000 steps

blocks.html:
When the input grows 10 times bigger, O(n) takes 10 times more steps, but O(n^2) takes 100 times more. That is why quadratic code becomes very slow on large data.

The O(log n) Idea

Some algorithms cut the problem in half again and again. If you have 1000 items and you throw away half each step, you need only about 10 steps. This is O(log n). Binary search uses this idea (you will meet it in the Sorting & Searching lesson).

blocks.output:
n = 8 -> halving steps: 3
n = 1024 -> halving steps: 10
n = 1000000 -> halving steps: 19

blocks.html:
Even for one million items we need only 19 halvings. Logarithmic growth is very slow, which is excellent.

Common Mistakes

  • Thinking Big-O is exact seconds. It only shows how fast the work grows.
  • Keeping small parts: write O(n), not O(3n + 5).
  • Forgetting hidden loops. A call like x in my_list is itself a loop of up to n steps.
  • Believing a loop inside a loop is always O(n^2). It depends on what each loop counts.

Key Points

  • An algorithm is a list of steps; a data structure stores the data it works on.
  • Big-O measures how the number of steps grows with input size n.
  • Order from best to worst: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n^2).
  • Drop constants and small terms: 3n + 5 becomes O(n).
  • One loop over the data is O(n); a loop inside a loop is usually O(n^2); halving the data each step is O(log n).

Arrays & Dynamic Lists

Arrays and Python Lists

An array stores items one after another in memory. Because the items sit side by side, the computer can jump straight to any position using its index. Indexes start at 0, so the first item is at index 0.

Python's list is a dynamic array. Dynamic means it can grow and shrink. When the hidden space is full, Python quietly gets a bigger block and copies the items across, so append is still fast on average.

blocks.code:
marks = [72, 85, 90, 64, 78]

print("first:", marks[0])
print("last:", marks[-1])
print("length:", len(marks))
print("slice:", marks[1:4])

marks[3] = 70          # change one item
marks.append(88)       # add at the end
print(marks)

blocks.html:
Cost of Each Operation

The cost depends on where you work in the list. Operations at the end are cheap. Operations at the front or in the middle must shift all the items after that position.

OperationCodeCost
Read by indexa[i]O(1)
Add at the enda.append(x)O(1) on average
Remove from the enda.pop()O(1)
Insert at position ia.insert(i, x)O(n)
Delete at position idel a[i]O(n)
Search for a valuex in aO(n)

blocks.code:
def insert_at(items, index, value):
    items.append(None)                    # make room
    shifts = 0
    for i in range(len(items) - 1, index, -1):
        items[i] = items[i - 1]           # shift right
        shifts += 1
    items[index] = value
    return shifts

nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print("shifts at front:", insert_at(nums, 0, 5))
print(nums)
print("shifts at end:", insert_at(nums, len(nums), 99))
print(nums)

blocks.html:
Inserting at the front moved all 5 items. Inserting at the end moved none. This is why we prefer adding at the end of a list.

2D Lists (Grids)

A list can hold other lists. A list of lists is a 2D list, like a table with rows and columns. Use grid[row][col] to read one cell. Be careful when you create one: [[0] * 3] * 2 repeats the same row twice, so changing one row changes both. Use a list comprehension to make separate rows.

blocks.code:
grid = [[1, 2, 3],
        [4, 5, 6],
        [7, 8, 9]]
print("row 1, col 2:", grid[1][2])
for row in grid:
    print(row, "sum =", sum(row))

bad = [[0] * 3] * 2            # same row twice
bad[0][0] = 1
print("bad: ", bad)

good = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]   # separate rows
good[0][0] = 1
print("good:", good)

blocks.html:
Common Mistakes

  • Using an index that is too big. For a list of 5 items the last index is 4, and a[5] raises IndexError.
  • Inserting or deleting at the front inside a big loop. Each one costs O(n), so the whole loop becomes O(n^2).
  • Building a grid with [[0] * 3] * 2. Use a list comprehension instead.

Key Points

  • A list stores items in order and each item has an index starting at 0.
  • Reading by index is O(1); append and pop at the end are fast.
  • Insert and delete in the front or middle are O(n) because items must shift.
  • A 2D list is a list of lists; read a cell with grid[row][col].
  • Create grids with a list comprehension so the rows are separate.

Stacks & Queues

Two Simple Rules

A stack and a queue are lists with strict rules about how items go in and come out. These rules make them simple and very useful.

  • Stack = LIFO (Last In, First Out). Think of a pile of plates: you add and remove from the top.
  • Queue = FIFO (First In, First Out). Think of a line at a ticket counter: the first person is served first.

Stacks are used for the undo button, the browser back button and function calls. Queues are used for printer jobs, customer lines and task scheduling.

A Stack with a List

A Python list works well as a stack. Use append to push and pop to remove the top. Both are O(1) at the end of the list.

blocks.code:
stack = []
stack.append("page1")     # push
stack.append("page2")
stack.append("page3")
print("stack:", stack)
print("top item:", stack[-1])
print("popped:", stack.pop())   # last in, first out
print("popped:", stack.pop())
print("left:", stack)
blocks.output:
stack: ['page1', 'page2', 'page3']
top item: page3
popped: page3
popped: page2
left: ['page1']

blocks.html:
A Queue with deque

You can use a list as a queue, but list.pop(0) is O(n) because every item shifts left. Python gives us collections.deque (double-ended queue). Its append and popleft are both O(1).

blocks.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque()
queue.append("Ali")        # enqueue
queue.append("Sara")
queue.append("Omar")
print("queue:", list(queue))
print("served:", queue.popleft())   # first in, first out
print("served:", queue.popleft())
print("waiting:", list(queue))
print("empty?", len(queue) == 0)
blocks.output:
queue: ['Ali', 'Sara', 'Omar']
served: Ali
served: Sara
waiting: ['Omar']
empty? False

blocks.html:
Example: Balanced Brackets

A compiler must check that every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket in the correct order. A stack solves this. Push each opening bracket. When you see a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its partner. At the end the stack must be empty.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling pop() on an empty list. It raises IndexError, so check if stack: first.
  • Using list.pop(0) for a queue. It works but it is slow for big data; use deque.popleft().
  • Forgetting the final check in the bracket example. The text "((a)" leaves one bracket behind, so the stack is not empty.

Key Points

  • Stack is LIFO: push and pop at the same end. Use a list with append and pop.
  • Queue is FIFO: add at the back, remove from the front. Use collections.deque.
  • Both main operations are O(1) when you use the right tool.
  • A stack checks balanced brackets, and also powers undo and function calls.

Linked Lists

Nodes Joined by Links

A linked list stores items in small objects called nodes. Each node holds a value and a link to the next node. The first node is the head, and the last node links to None. The nodes can be anywhere in memory, because the links connect them.

A Python list keeps items side by side and uses indexes. A linked list has no indexes: to reach the third node you must start at the head and follow two links.

blocks.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None      # link to the next node

a = Node(10)
b = Node(20)
c = Node(30)
a.next = b
b.next = c

current = a                   # start at the head
while current is not None:
    print(current.value)
    current = current.next

blocks.html:
A LinkedList Class

Now we wrap the nodes in a class. Adding at the head is O(1) because we only change two links. Adding at the tail needs a walk to the end, which is O(n). Deleting a value means we find the node before it and make that node skip over the unwanted node.

Linked List vs Array List

TaskPython listLinked list
Read item number iO(1)O(n)
Insert at the frontO(n)O(1)
Insert at the endO(1) on averageO(n) (O(1) if you keep a tail link)
Delete a node you already holdO(n)O(1) after you have found the previous node
Memory useOnly the valuesValue plus a link for every node

In everyday Python the built-in list is the best choice. Linked lists matter because they teach how links work, and the same idea builds trees and graphs.

blocks.code:
# Same task: build a list of 1..5 by always adding at the FRONT
arr = []
for x in range(1, 6):
    arr.insert(0, x)          # shifts every item: O(n) each time
print("python list:", arr)

head = None
for x in range(1, 6):
    head = (x, head)          # a tiny linked list made of pairs: O(1) each time
out = []
while head is not None:
    out.append(head[0])
    head = head[1]
print("linked pairs:", out)

blocks.html:
Common Mistakes

  • Losing the rest of the list. When you insert, set node.next first and then change the previous link.
  • Forgetting the empty-list case, where head is None.
  • Writing cur.next.value when cur.next is None. This raises AttributeError.

Key Points

  • A linked list is a chain of nodes; each node has a value and a next link.
  • The head is the first node; the last node points to None.
  • Insert at the head is O(1); search, traverse and insert at the tail are O(n).
  • Delete by making the previous node skip the unwanted node.
  • No indexes: you must walk from the head to reach a position.

Trees & Binary Search Trees

What is a Tree?

A tree is a data structure shaped like an upside-down real tree. It is made of nodes joined by links, but unlike a linked list, a node can have more than one child. Folders on your computer are a good example: a folder contains files and other folders.

WordMeaning
RootThe top node; it has no parent
Parent / childA node and the nodes directly below it
LeafA node with no children
SubtreeA node together with everything below it
HeightThe number of links on the longest path from the root down to a leaf

In a binary tree every node has at most two children, called left and right.

Binary Search Tree Rule

A binary search tree (BST) keeps its values in order using one rule: for every node, all values in the left subtree are smaller, and all values in the right subtree are bigger. To insert or search, compare with the current node, then go left or right. If the tree is balanced, each step throws away about half the nodes, so insert and search are O(log n).

blocks.output:
root: 50
left child: 30  right child: 70
search 60: True
search 65: False

blocks.html:
Inorder Traversal

Traversal means visiting every node. In inorder traversal we visit the left subtree, then the node itself, then the right subtree. On a BST this gives the values in sorted order, which is a nice free bonus of the BST rule.

The second tree has height 4 for only 5 values. It looks like a linked list, and searching it is O(n). Sorted input makes a BST lopsided. Real systems use self-balancing trees to avoid this problem.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting the base case if root is None in a recursive function. It leads to an AttributeError.
  • Forgetting to assign the result back: write root.left = insert(root.left, key).
  • Thinking every BST is fast. A BST built from sorted data is O(n) to search.

Key Points

  • A tree has a root, parents, children and leaves; a binary tree allows at most two children.
  • BST rule: left values are smaller, right values are bigger.
  • Insert and search are O(log n) on a balanced tree and O(n) on a lopsided one.
  • Inorder traversal (left, node, right) prints a BST in sorted order.
  • Trees are naturally recursive: each child is a smaller tree.

Hash Tables

Fast Lookup by Key

A hash table stores key-value pairs and finds a key in O(1) time on average. It does not search through all items. Instead it uses a hash function to turn the key into a number, and that number tells where to look.

The table is an array of buckets. To store a key we compute hash(key) % size, which gives a bucket index between 0 and size - 1. To read the key later, we compute the same index and go straight to that bucket.

blocks.output:
ali -> bucket 2
sara -> bucket 3
omar -> bucket 4
lahore -> bucket 5

blocks.html:
Collisions

Different keys can land in the same bucket. This is called a collision. It is normal, because there are many more possible keys than buckets. One common fix is chaining: each bucket holds a small list, and all keys with the same index go into that list. Lookup then hashes the key and checks only the short list.

Our simple hash adds letter codes, so "cat" and "act" always collide (same letters). Real hash functions mix the letters better.

You can see the collisions: "cat", "act" and "sun" all share bucket 2, yet each key is still found correctly.

Python's dict

You already use a hash table: Python's dict. It resizes itself and uses a strong hash function, so lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average. A set works the same way but stores only keys. Keys must be hashable, which means they cannot change: strings, numbers and tuples are fine, lists are not.

Common Mistakes

  • Believing the lookup is always O(1). With many collisions it can fall to O(n); good hash functions keep that rare.
  • Using a list as a dict key. Use a tuple instead.
  • Expecting a certain order. Treat a hash table as unordered lookup, not as a sorted structure.
  • Reading a missing key with d[key]. It raises KeyError; use d.get(key).

Key Points

  • A hash function turns a key into a number; % size picks the bucket.
  • Average cost of put, get and delete is O(1).
  • A collision is two keys in one bucket; chaining stores them together in a small list.
  • Python's dict and set are hash tables.
  • Keys must be hashable (unchangeable): strings, numbers, tuples.

Sorting & Searching

Searching a List

Linear search checks the items one by one from the start. It works on any list and costs O(n). Binary search works only on a sorted list. It looks at the middle item and throws away the half that cannot contain the target, so it costs O(log n). For one million items that is about 20 checks instead of up to one million.

Bubble Sort

Bubble sort is the simplest sorting idea. Go through the list and swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. After each pass the biggest unsorted item has bubbled to the end. It uses two loops, so it costs O(n^2). It is easy to understand but too slow for large lists.

Merge Sort and sorted()

Merge sort uses divide and conquer: split the list in half, sort each half by the same method, then merge the two sorted halves into one. The list is halved about log n times and each level does n work, so merge sort costs O(n log n), much better than O(n^2).

In real programs you simply call Python's built-in sorted() (or list.sort()). It is fast, well tested, and its worst case is O(n log n).

blocks.code:
def merge_sort(items):
    if len(items) <= 1:
        return items
    mid = len(items) // 2
    left = merge_sort(items[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(items[mid:])
    merged = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            merged.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    merged.extend(left[i:])
    merged.extend(right[j:])
    return merged

nums = [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]
print("merge_sort:", merge_sort(nums))
print("sorted()  :", sorted(nums))
print("reverse   :", sorted(nums, reverse=True))
print("by length :", sorted(["pear", "fig", "banana", "kiwi"], key=len))
print("original  :", nums)

blocks.html:
Comparing the Methods

MethodNeeds sorted data?Cost
Linear searchNoO(n)
Binary searchYesO(log n)
Bubble sortNoO(n^2)
Merge sortNoO(n log n)
sorted()NoO(n log n)

Common Mistakes

  • Using binary search on an unsorted list. The answer will be wrong.
  • Writing mid = (low + high) / 2. Use // so the index is a whole number.
  • Using low < high instead of low <= high. You may skip the last item.
  • Expecting list.sort() to return a list. It sorts in place and returns None; sorted() returns a new list.

Key Points

  • Linear search is O(n) and works on any list.
  • Binary search is O(log n) but needs a sorted list.
  • Bubble sort swaps neighbours and is O(n^2).
  • Merge sort splits, sorts and merges; it is O(n log n).
  • In real code use sorted().

Graphs, BFS & DFS

What is a Graph?

A graph is a set of vertices (also called nodes) joined by edges. Graphs model things that are connected: cities and roads, people in a social network, web pages and links. Unlike a tree, a graph can have loops and there is no single root.

The easiest way to store a graph in Python is an adjacency list: a dict where each key is a vertex and the value is the list of its neighbours. In an undirected graph, if A is connected to B then B is also connected to A, so we store both.

blocks.code:
graph = {
    "A": ["B", "C"],
    "B": ["A", "D", "E"],
    "C": ["A", "F"],
    "D": ["B"],
    "E": ["B", "F"],
    "F": ["C", "E"],
}

for vertex, neighbours in graph.items():
    print(vertex, "->", neighbours)

edges = sum(len(n) for n in graph.values()) // 2
print("vertices:", len(graph), " edges:", edges)

blocks.html:
Breadth-First Search (BFS)

BFS visits the start vertex, then all its neighbours, then the neighbours of those, and so on, spreading out layer by layer like ripples in water. It uses a queue. Because it reaches closer vertices first, BFS finds the path with the fewest edges.

Depth-First Search (DFS)

DFS goes as deep as possible along one path, and only when it is stuck does it go back (backtrack) and try another path. The easiest way to write it is with recursion, because the function-call stack remembers where to return. Both BFS and DFS cost O(V + E): each vertex and edge is handled once.

Compare the two results: BFS visited C early (it is close to A), but DFS went down the B branch first and reached C last.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting the visited check. In a graph with a loop, the search then runs forever.
  • Using a list as the BFS queue. pop(0) is O(n); use deque.
  • Storing an edge only one way in an undirected graph.
  • Mixing up the two: BFS uses a queue (layers), DFS uses recursion or a stack (deep paths).

Key Points

  • A graph is vertices joined by edges; store it as a dict of neighbour lists.
  • BFS uses a queue and explores layer by layer; it finds the fewest-edge path.
  • DFS goes deep first, usually with recursion, then backtracks.
  • Always remember visited vertices so loops do not repeat forever.
  • Both BFS and DFS take O(V + E) time.
